items.context: You work for a large company. You received this email from the Human Resources Manager.
items.situation: From September, staff will no longer have their own desks. Each morning, everyone will choose a free desk, and personal items must be kept in a locker overnight.

informal.prompt: Write an email to a colleague who is also a friend. Tell your colleague about the change and say how you feel about it. Write about 40–50 words.

b2.text:
Hi Nuria,

Did you read the email about the desks? From September nobody will have their own, and we have to clear everything away every evening! I'm not happy, because I like having my photos around me. Why don't we ask to sit together?

Best,
Ana

formal.prompt: Write an email to the Human Resources Manager. Give your opinion of the change and make some suggestions. Write 120–150 words.

b2.text:
Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing to give my opinion about the new desk system that will start in September.

I have worked in the marketing team for six years, and I like having a fixed desk. If I have to look for a free desk every morning, I will lose time before I can start working. I also need to be near my team, because we often work on projects together. Moreover, some colleagues may feel less comfortable if they cannot keep personal items at their desk.

I understand that the company wants to use the space better. However, I would like to suggest that each team has its own area, so that colleagues can sit together. It would also help to have a booking system.

I hope you will think about my suggestions.

Yours faithfully,
Ana Morales

c.text:
Dear Mr Allen,

I am writing in connection with the introduction of unassigned desks from September.

While I understand the rationale for making better use of office space, I am concerned that the new arrangement may undermine both productivity and morale. Not only will staff lose valuable time each morning searching for a free desk, but teams that depend on close collaboration will also be dispersed across the floor. Furthermore, being unable to personalise one's workspace can hardly be expected to boost motivation.

I would therefore propose that desks be allocated by team, with an online booking system to confirm seating in advance. Were a trial period to be introduced, staff could provide feedback before the policy is finalised.

I would appreciate it if you would take these suggestions into consideration.

Yours sincerely,
Ana Morales

note.en: A precise formal noun meaning 'the reasoning behind'.

formal.prompt: Write an email to the school director. Give your opinion of the change and make some suggestions. Write 120–150 words.

b2.text:
Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing to give my opinion about the new timetable that will start next term.

I have studied at the school for a year and I am very happy with my course. However, I cannot attend a three-hour class on Saturday mornings, because I work in a shop at weekends. I also think that three hours is too long, and students will be tired and will learn less. Short classes during the week are better for learning a language, as we can practise more often.

I understand that the school wants to organise the classrooms better. Therefore, I would like to suggest keeping at least one evening class during the week. Another idea is to divide the Saturday class into two parts with a break.

I hope you will consider my suggestions.

Yours faithfully,
Elena Ruiz

c.text:
Dear Ms Whitaker,

I am writing in response to your announcement that the Tuesday and Thursday evening classes will be replaced by a single Saturday morning session next term.

I appreciate that the current timetable is difficult to manage. Nevertheless, I feel that the proposed arrangement would not only exclude students who work at weekends, but also compromise the quality of learning. Languages are acquired through regular, spaced practice; a three-hour block, by contrast, is likely to result in fatigue and reduced retention.

So as to preserve both flexibility and effectiveness, I would recommend retaining one weekday evening class alongside a shorter Saturday session. Were the school to offer a choice of groups, I believe most students would welcome it.

I would be grateful if you could give this matter your careful consideration.

Yours sincerely,
Elena Ruiz

items.context: You are a member of a community garden. You received this email from the residents' association.

b2.text:
Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing to express my opposition to the plan to turn half of the community garden into a car park for the new health centre.

I have had a plot in the garden for six years and I grow vegetables for my family. The garden is also a place where neighbours meet, and it is important for children and older people in the area. If half of it disappears, many members will lose their plots, and the smaller plots offered next year will not be enough.

I understand that the health centre needs parking. However, there may be other solutions. For example, the car park could be built on the empty land behind the old depot, or the centre could encourage patients to use public transport.

I hope the association will think again.

Yours faithfully,
Mia Collins

c.text:
Dear Mr Dawson,

I am writing to register my objection to the proposal to convert the western half of the community garden into a car park for the new health centre.

The garden is more than a collection of allotments; it is a social and environmental asset for the whole neighbourhood. Under the proposal, not only would many members lose their plots, but the habitat that has developed over many years would also be destroyed. Moreover, the smaller plots offered next year would hardly compensate for such a loss.

While I recognise the need for adequate parking, it is the choice of site that I find difficult to accept. Might the association explore alternatives, such as unused land nearby? Should the plan nevertheless proceed, a binding commitment to protect the remaining land would be essential.

I would be grateful for the opportunity to discuss this.

Yours sincerely,
Mia Collins
